Yeah, I'm a little bit late.

There'S a.

Beverly Hills.

So thank you for booking him a call with me.
Obviously we, we can get into what you, why you're here and you know how we can help.

Obviously the nature of these calls really is to just dig into the business, figure out what it is that's going wrong and maybe spot what is going right and help sort of clarify a way of moving forward.
See I can, I can leave the floor for you to discuss all of that, but just a little bit of background about us.
So we were an M and A advisory as capital A.
We work on both sides of the table.
So we do a lot of buy side work as well for our clients who tend to be sort of either scaling agencies that are looking to acquire or private equity firms or investors.
And as well as that we have the agencies co platform for sellers.
So we work both sides of the table which means we get to see everything inside an agency and also just what generally agencies are worth and why they're worth what they are.
My background is also marketing and media and I sold my company in 2016 so kind of been there and felt the pain.
So, so great to hear about your company.
Sure, sure.
And what you do.
Yeah.
So we are a conversion rate optimization agency primarily for E Commerce brands.
We do a little bit of lead gen.
We have done SaaS in the past but I really tried to narrow down the scope to just E Commerce.
I certainly don't turn those lead gen or SaaS tools away from they come knocking.
But that's not my core competency, not what I've built my systems around.
So I started doing CRO.
I learned about it in 2001, ran my first A B test in 2003.
Became a consultant for an agency based out of San Francisco in 2012 and worked there until 2017.
And I left and started Surefoot with a partner.
My partner left in December of 2023.
I bought her out completely.
So I'm the sole owner now.
And we were doing really great.
Covid hit and we couldn't hire fast enough.
We got up to like forget now it was like 240mrr in July of 2022 and then interest rates started going up and we started losing clients left and right.

We had a lot of clients we didn't realize were on inventories were on loan or the loans, their inventory was on loans and their loans got called or they were VC backed and their VC dried up and interest rates went up and we went through a lot of layoffs over the course of like 18 months.
We just kept slowly declining and trying to like really hang on to the team thinking things Might turn around at any point.
And they didn't.
And we didn't pay ourselves very well during that decline because we were trying to keep the team together.
We built a really great team at that point.
And then from my partner Left just like 16 months ago, whatever it was.
At that point we'd gotten down to.
We'd been 18 people strong and the peak at 220mrr.
And then we got down to like four people.
From my partner left, it was me and three other people left.
And I'm back up to.
I actually just let one person go on Tuesday and it's been.
So we got down to about 60,000 mrr.
My partner left in December of 2023 and I've hovered around that like I've got up to 80, dropped back down, got back up, drop back down.
And my partner did all the sales.
I did ops and so I've been learning sales for the last year plus and in April last year.
So a year ago right now actually I started posting on LinkedIn two or three times a week and now I've been posting daily probably since May or June.
And then I added Twitter in October and I've been posting on there at least five times a week and just trying to grow an audience.
It has generated leads.
I started the newsletter in January.
It's a daily, every Sunday morning at 5:30.
It's a long thought piece about how to do like here's why you should do it, here's how to do it.
Here's a case study on what we've done, how we've done this for a client.
It's only got like 100 subscribers so far.
It's not that big.
LinkedIn I've got about 5,000 followers, mostly in the e commerce space.
In Twitter I've got like 2500.
That's just like a weird smattering of who knows what.
And December.
So we've had very inconsistent lead flow throughout our history.
We really relied mostly on referrals.

And then January I got eight.
February I got eight.
March I got eight.
This month I'm on track to have 12 qualified leads.
And it's like things are seem to be hitting pretty well.
January, I signed two new clients.
My goal this year was to sign two dinner two to three new clients every month.
But I didn't sign any more since then until yesterday.
I had two right away in January.
Thought I was going to come out hitting and Then I just couldn't close anything until Friday.
I had a, just, I had a Wednesday call last week that the discovery.
Friday I had a pitch and really just closed the pitch on Friday saying let's schedule the kickoff call.
You guys say you're ready to go.
If prices that hang up, we'll figure it out.
You know, if you believe in the roi, I'm going to get you then like why wait?
And so we scheduled the call for kickoff yesterday.
They finally reviewed the contract yesterday morning, gave me some feedback.
We changed the contract.
I've got to send it for signature here today.
But they're good to go.
Like we're locked in, we're off to the races.
And so I think it was just a matter of like unlocking a switch in my head about getting dogged with sales and not giving up on people, not letting them drive the calls.
Yeah, yeah.
Learning curve, isn't it?
So congratulations on breaking the dry spell because that is the most nerve wracking part, isn't it?

Are you making sure that you're following up with a ton of emails?
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
It sounds like you.

Sounds like thing.
Yeah, yeah.
So you've got a sequence, you were saying?

I've got a weekly touch base sequence and I make sure if anyone reaches out through the contact forms of my site, they're getting signed up for my newsletter.
So I get in front of them that way.
Yeah, I'm trying to make sure I always connect with any new leads on LinkedIn so they see my content there.
Yeah, just trying to get the marketing machine working and everything connected and, and talking to each other and.
Yeah, yeah, amazing.
I think you're doing a great job.
So what was the deal with your partner?
How much did you buy her out for?
Was it a lot of Money.
Where did you get it from?
So it was a 130,000.
We had a deal.

Because we.

And she wanted, like, a $300,000 buyout.
And I just didn't see how that would even make any sense.
And so we went back to the agreement.

And so we went and did that.
At that point, we didn't have any debt, but we just weren't very profitable at all.
We weren't paying ourselves much or anything like that.
And so we did the valuation.
It came back.
I took out all of the.
I backed out, like, expenses that hadn't been paid yet, taxes, all that kind of stuff.
And it left her with 132.

Wow.
Brilliant.
And so where have you got the game plan for your marketing from, given that you were the ops guy previously?
Yeah, so I joined a group called Hydra a year ago this month.
I went to their conference, actually, in Nashville, and I joined them, I think, in June of last year, if I remember correctly.
And one of the things they just talked about at the conference was like, you've got to be on LinkedIn.
You got to be on LinkedIn.
And then a friend of mine who also runs was running an agency.
He's left now.
He's still part owner, but he started his own e commerce business.
He told me, like, don't.
Don't do cold outreach.
Let them come to you.
It's much better for selling.
It's like, generate the content so people are coming to you and you're owning the thought space.
And so that's.
I just doubled down on all of it.
Yeah.
And how are you getting people in?
Are you.
Have you created a lead magnet to get people to come to you, or what's the process?
Yeah, so I did try a lead magnet that is really.
We really wrote out everything we do for our strategy, and we built a strategy tool.
We call it Usability Scorecard.
I'm going to change the name of it because no one cares about usability.
They care about revenue.

Yeah.

They've just been coming in from LinkedIn and Twitter and hitting my site and filling out my contact form on the site.
Yeah, that's the thing about the lead magnets.
You've got to show them what they need to do, but not how.
Yeah.
Then it doesn't really matter what you can tell them as much as you can you provide the how.
So.
Yeah, a bit scary if you've got competitors just downloading all of your stuff.
So anyway, look, let me just first say I'm really impressed with what you've just said about all of the marketing stuff.
I know another guy who does CRO in New York, you probably know him actually, but he's got a great Twitter and he's doing, he's been doing.
And he's probably been in the space.
Not so much in the space, but he's been marketing himself really well for the last four or five years.
And he's got hundreds of thousands of leads generated through that kind of.
You've done.
And all he does is he.
I mean, he's like religious about it.
Tweets every day, case studies like you're saying, you know, pictures of landing pages fixed, etc.
Yeah, he generates tons and tons of interest.
He actually came to me and said, I want to sell my agency for 10 million.
I said, mate, you're dreaming.
I mean he was probably doing about 1 or 2 million in revenue, so it was massively overpriced.

Wow.
But I think most of it was on the back end.
However.
He will get that back end.
But he was, he was kind of hockey sticking.
So.

And you've always done CRO.
Yeah.

There's one more like heard in the punch bowl.

They reshifted the budget, it went to someone else and they hired the IBM of CRO agencies.
I'm like, okay, you could have told me that as soon as it started happening because I hired someone.
But cool.
So I had someone working for me.
I had two account managers running all the clients.

So I got a loan thinking I could make the sales happen and couldn't.
Had to let her go and then have just been like chasing this, trying to get things going, spending money on marketing, whatever.

Yeah.

The repayment period.

About half.

Yeah.

No.
No.

What did you say?
17K was it?
Yeah.

Okay.

She's in freelance.

Yeah.

Three.

Okay, so your package that you're offering a new client, you get them on a conversation.
I mean give me your, your sales pitch.
What, what is it that you're selling?
A new client.
And what's the pack?
I mean not the whole thing but you know, what's the actual package that you're, you're giving them and what does it do for them?
So I will pitch well, I'll walk them through how we work and talk about how we are a bolt on team of five to help them get going right away.
There's no delay.
We get to test if they are on Shopify.
We'll Install the testing tool and the heat map tool and get everything going.
If they are not, or if they want their own devs to do it, we'll give them explicit instructions about how to do that.
We're going to get their GA4 tuned up and then we're going to have some low hanging fruit tests that we're going to pick right away.
So we just do like a visual audit of the site, going through GA4 a little bit, looking to the analytics there to look for holes.
And then we're going to do our usability scorecard, which is our big strategy piece.
And that's going to where we actually interview prospective customers of theirs and have them go through each page type on the site.
So homepage, category page, product detail page, cart checkout, all that.
And we're going to find all the points where people have confusion, frustration and friction.
And then we're going to ask them why they're having the fusion, confusion and friction and all that and figure out really, we write a problem statement, here's, here's the problem.
And then we reverse engineer that into a hypothesis for how to fix it.
That will generate three to six months of testing hypotheses for them.
It'll also generate some things that we just need to go fix right away that will immediately see some conversion rate bumps, revenue bumps, and then it's really about how fast do they want to go.
And so I've got a little ROI calculator I'll show them that has a crawl walk run plan.
And it's just the number of tests generally the industry average for winning Test rate is 20 to 25%.
So one out of four, one out of five tests will win.
When we run our test out of our usability scorecard, our win rate jumps from up to 40 to 44% win rate.
So it really increases the odds that we have wins and then increases the odds of increasing revenue for them.
And so we try to run as many.
We'll at least do that every six months, if not every quarter for a client just to help us with that roadmap and drive the strategy for them.

So.

summary.overview: In the Business Consultation meeting between Brian Schmitt, founder of the conversion rate optimization agency Surefoot, and Andy Day from an M&A advisory firm, they discussed key aspects of Surefoot's operations and growth strategies amidst recent challenges. Brian detailed his company’s history, highlighting its decline from a peak of 18 employees and $240K MRR to 4 staff and $60-80K MRR due to economic pressures. Their marketing strategies have evolved to include regular social media posts and newsletters, contributing to an increase in qualified leads. However, Brian faces challenges with business loans and a reduced team, prompting discussions on creating lead magnets and lower-cost entry services to bolster client acquisition. Andy provided actionable growth strategies, including establishing a usability scorecard as a service and focusing on high-value corporate clients. The meeting concluded with Brian setting specific action items for client engagement and marketing development while Andy committed to reviewing the session and suggesting further recommendations.
summary.short_summary: Brian Schmitt, founder of Surefoot, a conversion rate optimization agency, met with Andy Day from an M&A advisory firm to address the company's operational challenges and growth strategies. Brian shared that Surefoot has seen a decline from 18 employees and $240K MRR to just 4 staff and $60-80K MRR due to economic pressures. In response, they have adapted their marketing strategies to include regular social media posts and newsletters, which have led to a rise in qualified leads. However, Brian is facing difficulties with business loans and maintaining a reduced team, leading to discussions about creating lead magnets and lower-cost entry services to attract more clients. Andy suggested actionable growth strategies, such as establishing a usability scorecard as a service and targeting high-value corporate clients. The meeting concluded with Brian setting action items regarding client engagement and marketing, while Andy planned to provide further recommendations after reviewing the session.
